title: Court rules Trump can blacklist Anthropic for refusing to enable Claude features
content:
A US appeals court today approved the Department of Defense’s blacklisting of Anthropic technology. Judges decided the Trump administration had authority to blacklist Anthropic for withholding certain AI features from the military even if Anthropic had no malicious intent.
In a 2-1 ruling issued by the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, a panel of judges said the “case raises profoundly difficult questions about the appropriate military uses of an almost unimaginably powerful new technology.” The US “raises the deeply sobering prospect of overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and thus causing important military operations to fail. Anthropic raises the deeply sobering prospect of unconstrained AI models hallucinating inappropriate targets for lethal military force,” the ruling said.
Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “must determine how best to balance the competing risks,” the court said. “In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution. Accordingly, we deny the petitions for review.” The same court previously denied Anthropic’s emergency motion for a stay in April.
The two judges who ruled against Anthropic were both appointed by Trump and served in the first Trump administration. Judge Gregory Katsas was previously deputy counsel to the president, and Judge Neomi Rao served in the Trump administration’s Office of Management and Budget.
Two courts, two different decisions
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in March after it ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products and banned defense contractors from doing any business with Anthropic. Anthropic may appeal today’s ruling, either by asking for an en banc review with all of the appeals court judges or by petitioning the Supreme Court.
“We respectfully disagree with the court’s decision,” an Anthropic spokesperson told CNBC. “Another federal court has already held the government’s parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review.” Despite the ongoing legal battle, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick recently said the Trump administration and Anthropic have patched up their relationship and are “in tune.”

report.summary: A US appeals court ruled the Trump administration can blacklist Anthropic after it refused to enable certain Claude features for the military.
report.background: The ruling stems from a clash between the Defense Department and Anthropic over military use of advanced AI. After Anthropic withheld certain Claude capabilities from the military, the Trump administration ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic products and barred defense contractors from doing business with the company. Anthropic sued in March, arguing the blacklisting was unlawful. A D.C. Circuit panel had already denied an emergency stay in April. In a 2-1 decision, the appeals court found the defense secretary did not exceed authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution. The majority judges, both Trump appointees, framed the case as a difficult balance between AI models that shut down and models that hallucinate lethal targets. Anthropic says another federal court already found a parallel designation unlawful.
key_points: The D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic's petitions for review in a 2-1 ruling, holding that the Trump administration had authority under the Supply Chain Security Act and the Constitution to blacklist Anthropic. The majority said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not transgress legal limits when balancing military AI risks. The two judges in the majority were appointed by Trump and served in his first administration.

The court described competing dangers: overly constrained AI models could shut down unexpectedly and cause military operations to fail, while unconstrained models could hallucinate inappropriate targets for lethal force. It said Trump and Hegseth must decide how best to balance those risks, effectively deferring to executive branch judgment on military AI deployment.

Anthropic sued in March after the administration ordered federal agencies to stop using its products and banned defense contractors from doing business with it. The same appeals court previously denied Anthropic's emergency stay motion in April. Anthropic disagrees with the ruling and may seek an en banc review or petition the Supreme Court.

Despite the legal defeat, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick recently said the Trump administration and Anthropic have repaired their relationship and are 'in tune.' That suggests the dispute may be both a legal fight over procurement authority and a political negotiation over how frontier AI is used in defense.
report.impact: The decision gives the US government broad leverage over AI vendors that resist military applications, potentially chilling safety-first policies at frontier labs. Companies may need clearer legal strategies for dual-use refusals, while defense contractors must assess supply-chain exposure. For developers, it signals that government contracts can override or conflict with internal usage limits, making compliance and policy design more fraught. For regular users, Claude availability in federal and defense contexts may remain restricted, and the case could shape how much say AI makers have over military use. Anthropic's expected appeal means the final rules are still unsettled, but the immediate precedent favors executive authority.
report.tools: Follow Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy and usage policies, plus court filings via PACER or CourtListener. For AI safety evaluation, watch open-source tools such as HELM, lm-evaluation-harness, OpenAI Evals, and Garak. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and DoD CDAO guidance are useful for understanding military AI governance and supply-chain risk.
